items.title: Use the main labelled search input on a shopping site
items.description: Find the primary search input by its accessible label rather than scanning visual position.
items.content: On shopping sites the main search box is the input with an accessible label naming the site (e.g. 'Search <site>'); submitting via Enter after typing is the most reliable form-submit path.

items.title: Dismiss EU cookie banners before interacting with results
items.description: Cookie consent overlays intercept early clicks on result tiles and should be handled first.
items.content: On EU domains, a cookie consent overlay typically blocks pointer events for the first interaction; dismissing or accepting it before the first click on a result tile avoids spurious mis-clicks and stuck-detector aborts.

query: Browse a results page for an item

items.title: Scroll once to surface the Sponsored vs Organic split
items.description: A single scroll past the first results reveals the sponsored-versus-organic boundary that aids disambiguation.
items.content: When the desired item is not on the first results page, scrolling once is usually enough to surface a Sponsored vs Organic split that helps disambiguation between paid placement and ranked organic matches.

items.title: Handling Search Result Pages as Landing Pages
items.description: The agent successfully navigates a site that redirects to search results instead of an intermediate product detail page.
items.content: When targeting specific products on e-commerce platforms, it is critical to first identify whether the landing page is already populated with search results; attempting to fill input fields directly on such pages may result in errors if the browser does not detect the active input element without scrolling.

items.title: Prioritize Scroll Actions Over Immediate Input Attempts
items.description: When navigating to a search results page where query inputs are unavailable or obscured, scrolling is more effective than immediate text entry actions.
items.content: The trajectory demonstrates that successful navigation often requires manual scrolling to reveal hidden elements like the search bar before attempting to type into it, rather than assuming input fields are immediately accessible upon page load.

items.title: Robustness in Handling Repeated Parse Failures
items.description: The agent persists with a plan even after encountering multiple consecutive failures, indicating a need for robust error handling and retry mechanisms.
items.content: A successful trajectory implies that the system must remain stable despite repeated parse failures when executing automated inputs, requiring fallback strategies like scrolling or waiting for page states to stabilize before retrying input actions.

items.title: Robustness Against Search Query Syntax Variations
items.description: The agent successfully navigated a target page but failed when attempting to simulate typing search terms with incorrect action syntax, resulting in repeated failures and an eventual time-out.
items.content: This trajectory highlights that the system relies heavily on correct action formatting; even successful navigation to the goal page does not guarantee success if subsequent user actions (like typing) are malformed or unsupported by the parsing engine. Future tasks should ensure search queries are executed with valid syntax before proceeding.

items.title: Mitigation Strategies for Infinite Scrolling Loops
items.description: The agent encountered a stuck state where it repeated an invalid action five times, triggering a stuck-detector timeout that aborted the run prematurely.
items.content: Repeated scrolling or clicking without interaction yielded diminishing results and eventually triggered a safety mechanism to stop the process. Successful agents should implement loops with strict iteration limits (e.g., 3-5 attempts) and incorporate fallback strategies like switching actions or retrying previous steps upon detecting redundancy.

items.title: Separation of Navigation and Interaction States
items.description: The agent reached the search results page but failed to retrieve relevant items due to an inability to parse and execute specific typing commands, leading to a timeout.
items.content: Success depends not only on reaching the correct destination but also on executing valid user interactions within that context; if an interaction fails immediately upon entry or persists after navigation, it may indicate a fundamental limitation in the system's capability for that specific task type rather than a lack of effort.

items.title: Avoidance of Non-Interactive Element Parsing
items.description: Relying on a specific search query string that results in consistent parse failures indicates the interaction target does not support direct text input.
items.content: When an action involving text entry triggers immediate parsing errors regardless of retries or preceding clicks, it suggests the current interface lacks the necessary interactive field for that operation. Future attempts should verify the presence of a valid text input element before initiating a search query action on unrelated pages.

items.title: Implementation of Adaptive Query Execution Strategies
items.description: Repeating a failed interaction pattern without varying the approach is an inefficient use of resources and fails to address potential interface constraints.
items.content: If an initial attempt to perform an action (such as typing) results in failure, subsequent iterations should prioritize investigating alternative execution methods rather than executing the same sequence repeatedly. This strategy allows agents to identify valid paths by testing different combinations of interactions, such as clicking specific navigation elements before attempting text entry.

items.title: Recognition of Stuck-Loop Patterns for Early Detection
items.description: Observing that an agent remains in a state of failure after multiple repetitions provides valuable context regarding the robustness of the interaction path.
items.content: A persistent sequence of identical errors indicates that the chosen path is likely blocked by structural or functional limitations of the target interface. Agents should be configured to detect such repetitive loops and abort execution early, thereby preserving resources for re-evaluation of alternative strategies instead of continuing down a dead-end trajectory.

items.title: Preventing Infinite Retry Loops on Failed Actions
items.description: Avoid executing the exact same failed action repeatedly without introducing variation or switching strategies.
items.content: When an action fails due to a syntax error (such as incorrect search key format), the agent should immediately attempt a corrective measure like adjusting the parameter or selecting an alternative input method rather than re-executing the identical operation, which prevents the task from being aborted by stuck detection mechanisms.

items.title: Prioritizing Correct Parameter Syntax Before Execution
items.description: Ensure that all command parameters and formatting rules are verified and correct before triggering any user interaction function.
items.content: Agents must validate their action definitions against system requirements prior to submission; failing this check results in immediate parse failure, making it crucial to prioritize syntax correction over repeated execution attempts.

items.title: Implementing Adaptive Strategy Switches Upon Failure
items.description: When a search or input action fails, dynamically alter the approach by either changing the command structure or switching to a different functional pathway rather than cycling through identical actions.
items.content: Effective navigation requires an adaptive response loop where failure triggers a strategic pivot—such as verifying arguments, selecting alternate input methods, or revising the query format—rather than a static cycle of repeating a doomed strategy.
